body:
Why environmental protection requires international agreements

Environmental problems do not always remain within national boundaries. Air pollutants can travel across countries, rivers may flow through several nations, migratory animals cross international borders, and hazardous substances may be traded or transported from one country to another. Activities carried out in one country can therefore affect the environment and people elsewhere.

A country can regulate activities within its territory through national laws. However, problems involving shared resources, international trade or pollution crossing national boundaries also require cooperation among governments. Countries establish common rules, exchange information and undertake coordinated action through multilateral environmental agreements.

Multilateral environmental agreement

A multilateral environmental agreement is an agreement among multiple countries to cooperate on environmental protection, conservation or the sustainable use of natural resources. The obligations of each country depend on the particular agreement and the provisions it has accepted.

The depletion of stratospheric ozone illustrates this need. Scientists observed serious ozone depletion over Antarctica during the 1980s. Chemicals released in different parts of the world contributed to damage in the stratosphere. Protecting the ozone layer required countries to act together rather than independently.

Different environmental problems require different agreements

International environmental conventions can be understood by identifying the problem they address and the method they use to address it.

  • Ozone depletion: The Vienna Convention and Montreal Protocol address protection of the ozone layer. The Kigali Amendment extends the Montreal Protocol's controls to certain powerful greenhouse gases.
  • Hazardous chemicals and wastes: Basel regulates international movements of hazardous and certain other wastes; Rotterdam addresses international trade in specified hazardous chemicals; Stockholm controls persistent organic pollutants; Minamata addresses mercury.
  • Biodiversity and wildlife: CBD provides a broad framework for biodiversity conservation and sustainable use; CITES regulates international wildlife trade; CMS addresses migratory species; Ramsar focuses on wetlands.
  • Climate change and land degradation: UNFCCC concerns greenhouse gases and climate change, while UNCCD focuses on desertification, land degradation in drylands and the effects of drought.

Convention, protocol and amendment

The words convention, protocol and amendment describe different forms of international legal instruments. A convention is generally an international agreement establishing a framework or substantive obligations. A protocol is an agreement that may add more detailed obligations under a wider convention or treaty system. An amendment changes an existing treaty.

For example, the Vienna Convention of 1985 established cooperation for protecting the ozone layer. The Montreal Protocol of 1987 introduced specific controls on ozone-depleting substances. The Kigali Amendment of 2016 amended the Montreal Protocol to control hydrofluorocarbons. Kigali is therefore an amendment, not an unrelated convention.

Understanding treaty dates and membership

International agreements have several important dates. They should not be treated as interchangeable.

TermMeaning
AdoptionThe treaty text is formally agreed upon.
SignatureA country signs the treaty, generally indicating its intention to consider becoming bound by it.
RatificationA country formally expresses consent to be bound, usually after completing its domestic approval procedures.
AccessionA country joins through a formal act of consent without necessarily having signed the treaty earlier.
Entry into forceThe treaty becomes legally operative according to its specified conditions.
PartyA country or other eligible participant for which the treaty is legally in force.

A country may ratify a treaty in one year while the treaty enters into force for that country later. Similarly, a treaty may have been adopted decades before a particular country joined it.

Signing a treaty does not ordinarily mean that a country has completed ratification or become a Party. Also distinguish the treaty's global entry-into-force date from the date on which it becomes effective for India.

As of the content cutoff of 1 November 2026, India is a Party to every convention covered in this lesson and has ratified the Kigali Amendment. Their adoption years and India's joining years are different and must be learned separately.

How countries implement environmental conventions

Many conventions establish a Conference of the Parties (COP), where participating governments review implementation and make decisions within the treaty's rules. A secretariat provides administrative and technical support. Countries implement their commitments through national laws, policies, institutions, reporting and cooperation with other Parties, according to the requirements of each agreement.

International agreements do not automatically replace every national environmental rule. They establish obligations that countries must fulfil using the legal and administrative arrangements applicable to them.

Prelims focus

  • A multilateral environmental agreement involves cooperation among multiple countries.
  • Adoption, entry into force and India's joining date are distinct facts.
  • Ratification and accession are different ways of expressing consent to be bound.
  • Kigali is an amendment to the Montreal Protocol, not a separate convention.
  • Trap: A treaty's signature alone does not ordinarily establish full Party status.

[References: NCERT, Contemporary World Politics, Class 12, Chapter 8, Environment and Natural Resources, PDF pp. 118–124 in GPSC Volume 22; NCERT, Indian Economic Development, Class 11, Chapter 9, Environment and Sustainable Development, PDF pp. 167–170 in GPSC Volume 25; UNEP InforMEA, India, Party Status; UNEP Ozone Secretariat, India Country Profile; online sources consulted 1 November 2026.]

title: International Environmental Conventions: Meaning, Purpose and Classification

body:
Why the ozone layer needs protection

Ozone is a form of oxygen containing 3 oxygen atoms, represented as O3. Its environmental significance depends on where it is found. Stratospheric ozone, located high in the atmosphere, absorbs much of the Sun's harmful ultraviolet radiation. By contrast, ground-level ozone is an air pollutant that can damage human health and vegetation.

Substances such as chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs), which were widely used in refrigeration and other applications, can reach the stratosphere. Ultraviolet radiation breaks down these substances and releases reactive chlorine. Chlorine can repeatedly participate in reactions that destroy ozone molecules. A thinner ozone layer allows more harmful ultraviolet radiation, particularly UV-B, to reach the Earth's surface.

The international response developed through 3 related legal instruments: the Vienna Convention, the Montreal Protocol and the Kigali Amendment.

Vienna Convention for the Protection of the Ozone Layer, 1985

The Vienna Convention was adopted in 1985 and entered into force in 1988. It provides a framework for international cooperation in protecting the ozone layer. Its important functions include scientific research, systematic observation, exchange of information and cooperation on appropriate measures.

The Convention did not itself establish the detailed, quantified phase-out schedules for ozone-depleting chemicals. Those controls were developed through the Montreal Protocol.

India acceded to the Vienna Convention on 18 March 1991.

Montreal Protocol on Substances that Deplete the Ozone Layer, 1987

The Montreal Protocol was adopted in 1987 and entered into force in 1989. It established legally binding controls to phase out the production and consumption of specified ozone-depleting substances.

The controlled substances include CFCs, halons and other listed chemicals. Hydrochlorofluorocarbons (HCFCs) were also brought under control. Different substances and groups of countries have had different schedules and obligations under the Protocol.

For treaty purposes, consumption is a technical measure broadly calculated from production plus imports minus exports, subject to the Protocol's specific definitions and exclusions. Thus, the Montreal Protocol is not merely a general instruction to reduce visible emissions. It regulates the production and consumption of controlled substances.

The Protocol provides different implementation schedules for developed and eligible developing countries, along with financial and technical assistance arrangements for eligible developing countries.

India acceded to the Montreal Protocol on 19 June 1992.

Kigali Amendment to the Montreal Protocol, 2016

The Kigali Amendment was adopted in 2016 in Kigali, Rwanda, and entered into force internationally in 2019. It extends the Montreal Protocol's control system to hydrofluorocarbons (HFCs).

HFCs became important substitutes for some ozone-depleting substances in refrigeration, air-conditioning and other uses. Unlike CFCs, HFCs do not deplete the ozone layer. However, many HFCs are powerful greenhouse gases that contribute to global warming.

The Kigali Amendment therefore requires a phase-down of the production and consumption of listed HFCs. A phase-down means reducing quantities according to agreed schedules; it should not be confused with an immediate worldwide prohibition on every HFC.

India ratified the Kigali Amendment on 27 September 2021.

The 3 instruments compared

InstrumentAdoptedMain purposeIndia's status
Vienna Convention1985Scientific cooperation and framework for ozone protectionAcceded in 1991
Montreal Protocol1987Phase-out of controlled ozone-depleting substancesAcceded in 1992
Kigali Amendment2016Phase-down of listed HFCs because of their climate impactRatified in 2021

Ozone depletion is not the same as global warming

Montreal originally targeted chemicals that destroy stratospheric ozone. Kigali addresses HFCs mainly because of their contribution to global warming. Both are part of the Montreal Protocol system, but their immediate environmental purposes differ.

Applying the distinction

A question about scientific monitoring and international cooperation for ozone protection points to the Vienna Convention. A question about eliminating production and consumption of CFCs points to the Montreal Protocol. A question about reducing HFC use because these gases trap heat points to the Kigali Amendment.

Prelims focus

  • Vienna Convention: 1985; India acceded in 1991.
  • Montreal Protocol: 1987; internationally effective in 1989; India acceded in 1992.
  • Kigali Amendment: 2016; internationally effective in 2019; India ratified in 2021.
  • Montreal controls listed ozone-depleting substances; Kigali phases down listed HFCs.
  • Trap: HFCs are greenhouse gases but are not ozone-depleting substances.

[References: NCERT, Biology, Class 12, Chapter 16, Environmental Issues, Section 16.7, Ozone Depletion in the Stratosphere, PDF pp. 307–308 in GPSC Volume 35; UNEP Ozone Secretariat, The Montreal Protocol on Substances that Deplete the Ozone Layer, treaty overview; UNEP Ozone Secretariat, Kigali Story, adoption and entry into force; UNEP Ozone Secretariat, India Country Profile, Status of Ratification; online sources consulted 1 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: CFCs release chlorine that repeatedly destroys stratospheric ozone, increasing UV-B exposure; HFCs retain heat and contribute to warming without depleting ozone.
pictures.caption: Ozone depletion and HFC-related global warming involve different atmospheric effects.

title: Ozone Protection: Vienna Convention, Montreal Protocol and Kigali Amendment

body:
Why hazardous substances need different international controls

Hazardous substances can cause harm at different stages of their life cycle. A chemical may be dangerous when manufactured or used, when traded internationally, when released into the environment or when discarded as waste.

These different situations explain why there are separate environmental conventions for waste shipments, international chemical trade, persistent pollutants and mercury. Their subjects overlap in environmental protection, but their main legal mechanisms differ.

Basel Convention, 1989: Transboundary movement of hazardous wastes

The Basel Convention on the Control of Transboundary Movements of Hazardous Wastes and Their Disposal was adopted in 1989 in Basel, Switzerland, and entered into force in 1992.

Its central purpose is to protect human health and the environment from the harmful effects of hazardous and certain other wastes. It seeks to minimize hazardous-waste generation, promote environmentally sound waste management and regulate waste movement from one country to another.

A key mechanism is prior informed consent. Before a regulated transboundary waste movement proceeds, the competent authorities of the importing and transit States must be notified, and written import consent and any required written transit consent must be obtained. The shipment must also satisfy the Convention's conditions for environmentally sound management.

Basel does not simply mean that every international shipment of every type of waste is prohibited. Its rules control specified waste movements, and certain movements are prohibited under particular provisions or applicable amendments.

India ratified the Basel Convention on 24 June 1992.

Rotterdam Convention, 1998: Prior informed consent for listed chemicals

The Rotterdam Convention on the Prior Informed Consent Procedure for Certain Hazardous Chemicals and Pesticides in International Trade was adopted in 1998 and entered into force in 2004.

Its most distinctive feature is the Prior Informed Consent (PIC) procedure. For chemicals listed in Annex III, importing Parties communicate decisions on whether they permit future imports and, where applicable, under what conditions. Exporting Parties must ensure that their exporters comply with those decisions.

The Convention concerns specified hazardous industrial chemicals and pesticides in international trade. It is not a general treaty banning every hazardous chemical. Its purpose is to promote informed decisions and shared responsibility in chemical trade.

India acceded to the Rotterdam Convention on 24 May 2005.

Basel and Rotterdam both involve consent, but for different subjects

Basel regulates transboundary movement of hazardous and certain other wastes. Rotterdam uses the PIC procedure for international trade in specified hazardous chemicals and pesticides. The existence of consent requirements under both agreements does not make their coverage identical.

Stockholm Convention, 2001: Persistent organic pollutants

The Stockholm Convention on Persistent Organic Pollutants was adopted in 2001 and entered into force in 2004.

Persistent organic pollutants (POPs) are chemicals of international concern because they remain in the environment for long periods, can travel considerable distances, can accumulate in living organisms and may have harmful effects on health and ecosystems.

The Convention requires measures to eliminate or restrict listed POPs and to reduce releases of unintentionally produced POPs. Its annexes distinguish the main forms of control:

  • Annex A: Elimination of listed chemicals, subject to permitted exemptions.
  • Annex B: Restriction of listed chemicals for specified acceptable purposes or exemptions.
  • Annex C: Reduction of releases of listed chemicals produced unintentionally.

DDT is a useful example of an important qualification. It is listed under Annex B and may be used for disease-vector control when locally safe, effective and affordable alternatives are unavailable, in accordance with World Health Organization recommendations and guidelines and after notification to the Secretariat. It is therefore inaccurate to claim that the Stockholm Convention imposes an unconditional prohibition on every use of every listed POP.

India ratified the Stockholm Convention on 13 January 2006.

Minamata Convention, 2013: Mercury pollution

The Minamata Convention on Mercury was adopted in 2013 and entered into force in 2017. It is named after Minamata in Japan, where severe mercury pollution caused widespread illness.

Mercury can harm human health and the environment. The Convention addresses anthropogenic mercury pollution through measures concerning mercury supply and trade, specified mercury-added products and processes, emissions and releases, and environmentally sound management of mercury waste.

Its distinguishing feature is that it deals specifically with mercury and mercury compounds across important stages of their life cycle.

India ratified the Minamata Convention on 18 June 2018.

Comparison of the 4 conventions

ConventionAdoptedCore subjectIndia's status
Basel1989Hazardous and certain other waste movementsRatified in 1992
Rotterdam1998International trade in listed hazardous chemicals and pesticidesAcceded in 2005
Stockholm2001Persistent organic pollutantsRatified in 2006
Minamata2013Mercury and mercury compoundsRatified in 2018

Identifying the applicable convention

Consider a company exporting regulated hazardous industrial waste for disposal. The relevant international agreement is Basel. If a country must communicate whether it accepts imports of a chemical listed under the PIC procedure, the agreement is Rotterdam.

If a question describes a toxic organic chemical that persists, accumulates in organisms and travels long distances, Stockholm is the relevant convention. If the issue concerns mercury-added products or mercury emissions, the appropriate convention is Minamata.

One substance or shipment may be subject to more than one legal instrument if it meets their respective conditions. The correct convention in a question therefore depends on the activity being regulated, not merely on whether the substance is described as hazardous.

Prelims focus

  • Basel: 1989; transboundary movement of hazardous wastes; India ratified in 1992.
  • Rotterdam: 1998; PIC procedure for listed hazardous chemicals and pesticides; India acceded in 2005.
  • Stockholm: 2001; POPs; India ratified in 2006.
  • Minamata: 2013; mercury; India ratified in 2018.
  • Stockholm Annex A concerns elimination, Annex B restriction and Annex C unintentionally produced POPs.
  • Trap: Rotterdam does not automatically prohibit all international chemical trade.

[References: Basel Convention Secretariat, The Convention, Overview and History, adoption and control of transboundary movements; Rotterdam Convention Secretariat, The Convention, Overview and How It Works, PIC procedure, and Parties and Signatories, India; Stockholm Convention Secretariat, The Convention, Overview and History, and Annexes A–C; Minamata Convention on Mercury, Convention overview and India Party Profile; Government of India, Press Information Bureau, release 1488369, Basel, Rotterdam and Stockholm Conventions; UNEP InforMEA, India, Party Status; online sources consulted 1 November 2026.]

body:
Why biodiversity conservation is broader than species protection

Biodiversity refers to the variety of living organisms and the ecological systems of which they are part. It includes diversity within species, between species and among ecosystems. Protecting biodiversity therefore requires more than preventing the extinction of individual animals.

Biodiversity can be threatened by habitat destruction, overexploitation, invasive alien species and other harmful changes. Conservation may involve protecting natural habitats, managing biological resources sustainably and conserving species outside their natural habitats when necessary.

Convention on Biological Diversity, 1992

The Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD) was opened for signature at the United Nations Conference on Environment and Development, commonly called the Rio Earth Summit, in 1992. It entered into force in 1993.

The CBD has 3 objectives:

  1. Conservation of biological diversity: Protecting diversity at genetic, species and ecosystem levels.
  2. Sustainable use of its components: Using biological resources in ways that do not cause their long-term decline.
  3. Fair and equitable sharing of benefits: Sharing benefits arising from the utilization of genetic resources according to the Convention's provisions.

The third objective is an important distinction. CBD is concerned not only with protecting species but also with how benefits from genetic resources are shared.

For example, conserving a forest ecosystem addresses biodiversity conservation. Using its biological resources without undermining their continued existence concerns sustainable use. The terms on which genetic resources are accessed and their benefits shared concern the Convention's third objective.

India ratified the CBD in 1994 and became a Party on 19 May 1994.

The CBD has 3 objectives: conservation, sustainable use, and fair and equitable benefit sharing from genetic resources. Reducing it to wildlife protection alone leaves out important parts of the Convention.

Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora, 1973

CITES was adopted in 1973 in Washington and entered into force in 1975. It regulates international trade in specimens of listed wild animals and plants so that such trade does not threaten their survival.

In CITES, a specimen may include a live or dead animal or plant and, where covered by the Convention, its parts or derivatives. The Convention operates through a system of permits and certificates, with controls depending on the appendix in which the species is listed.

The 3 CITES appendices

  • Appendix I: Includes species threatened with extinction that are or may be affected by trade. International trade in their specimens is permitted only in exceptional circumstances. Trade for primarily commercial purposes is generally prohibited.
  • Appendix II: Includes species that are not necessarily threatened with extinction now but may become so unless trade is closely controlled, along with certain other species needed for effective regulation. International trade is permitted subject to applicable controls and documentation. Exports generally require an export permit based on legal acquisition and a finding that export will not be detrimental to the species' survival; re-exports require a re-export certificate.
  • Appendix III: Includes species protected in at least 1 country that has requested the cooperation of other Parties in controlling international trade.

Appendix II should not be interpreted as a list containing only species already endangered. Its purpose includes regulating trade before the affected species become threatened with extinction.

India ratified CITES on 20 July 1976. It entered into force for India on 18 October 1976.

CBD and CITES: Related but not identical

Both agreements contribute to biodiversity conservation, but they work differently. CBD establishes a broad framework covering conservation, sustainable use and benefit sharing. CITES specifically regulates international trade in specimens of species included in its appendices.

For example, managing a forest to conserve its biodiversity primarily relates to CBD's conservation objective. Exporting a specimen of a CITES-listed species involves CITES trade controls. A single conservation project or species may be relevant to both agreements, but their functions remain distinct.

CBD: Conservation, sustainable use and genetic-resource benefit sharing.
CITES: International trade in listed wild animals, plants and their covered specimens.

Prelims focus

  • CBD: 1992; opened for signature at the Rio Earth Summit; India became a Party in 1994.
  • CBD has 3 objectives, including fair and equitable benefit sharing.
  • CITES: 1973; adopted in Washington; India ratified in 1976.
  • CITES has 3 appendices with different international trade controls.
  • Trap: Appendix II species are not necessarily already threatened with extinction.

[References: NCERT, Biology, Class 12, Chapter 15, Biodiversity and Conservation, Sections 15.1.4 and 15.2, PDF pp. 289–293 in GPSC Volume 35; Convention on Biological Diversity Secretariat, Convention Text, Article 1, Objectives, and India Country Profile; CITES Secretariat, How CITES Works, Appendices I, II and III, and India Country Profile; online sources consulted 1 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: CITES appendices distinguish extinction-related restrictions, preventive trade regulation, and cooperation requested by a protecting country.
pictures.caption: The 3 CITES appendices impose different levels and purposes of international trade control.

title: Biodiversity and Wildlife Trade: CBD and CITES

body:
Why migratory animals need international protection

Many wild animals move seasonally between breeding, feeding, resting and wintering areas. Such movements may take them across several countries. Protecting a species in only 1 part of its range may be insufficient if it faces threats elsewhere along its migratory route.

The conservation of migratory species therefore requires cooperation among the countries that share their range. Wetlands are especially important in many bird migration routes because they provide feeding, resting and wintering habitats.

Convention on the Conservation of Migratory Species of Wild Animals, 1979

The Convention on Migratory Species (CMS) was adopted in 1979 in Bonn, Germany. It is also called the Bonn Convention. It entered into force in 1983.

CMS promotes cooperation among the Range States through which migratory animals move. Conservation measures may concern protection of species, maintenance or restoration of habitats, and coordinated responses to threats across the animals' migratory ranges.

The 2 CMS appendices

  • Appendix I: Lists endangered migratory species. Parties that are Range States undertake strict conservation obligations, including protection against taking except under the Convention's permitted exceptions and efforts to conserve and restore important habitats. Exceptions concern scientific purposes, enhancing propagation or survival, traditional subsistence needs or extraordinary circumstances; they must be precisely defined and limited in space and time and should not disadvantage the species.
  • Appendix II: Lists migratory species with an unfavourable conservation status that need international agreements for their conservation and management, or species that would significantly benefit from international cooperation.

A migratory species may appear in both appendices when the applicable criteria are satisfied. The lists should not be treated as mutually exclusive.

India has been a Party to CMS since 1 November 1983.

Ramsar Convention on Wetlands, 1971

The Ramsar Convention was adopted in 1971 at Ramsar in Iran and entered into force in 1975. Its official name is the Convention on Wetlands of International Importance especially as Waterfowl Habitat.

The Convention provides a framework for the conservation and wise use of wetlands. Wetlands include ecosystems such as marshes, lakes, floodplains and other qualifying natural or human-made wetland areas.

Wise use means maintaining the ecological character of wetlands through ecosystem-based approaches within the context of sustainable development. It does not necessarily mean excluding all human activities. It means ensuring that use and management are compatible with maintaining the wetland's ecological character.

Parties designate suitable wetlands for inclusion in the List of Wetlands of International Importance, commonly called the Ramsar List. Each Party must designate at least 1 wetland when joining. However, the Convention's wise-use principle applies to wetlands more broadly, not only to sites already included on the List.

The Ramsar Convention entered into force for India on 1 February 1982.

CMS and Ramsar address different subjects

CMS focuses on migratory animals and international cooperation across their ranges. Ramsar focuses on wetland ecosystems and their conservation and wise use.

A migratory bird may depend on several wetlands during its annual journey. Its conservation may involve CMS cooperation between Range States, while protection and wise use of its wetland habitats may involve Ramsar principles. The 2 conventions can therefore complement each other without having identical purposes.

Gujarat connections

Nalsarovar Bird Sanctuary

Nalsarovar Bird Sanctuary in Gujarat was designated as a Ramsar Site in 2012. Its significance includes wetland habitat for waterbirds. It illustrates how an Indian wetland can receive international recognition under Ramsar.

Chhari Dhand, Kachchh

Chhari Dhand in Gujarat has a Ramsar designation date of 16 June 2025; its addition to the List was announced on 30 January 2026. It is a seasonal saline wetland situated between the Banni grasslands and the salt flats of Kachchh. Seasonal flooding creates important habitat for wildlife, including wintering waterbirds.

The Ramsar Secretariat reported that India had 103 Ramsar Sites on 15 October 2026, a figure also shown in its country profile consulted at the 1 November 2026 content cutoff. Unlike the Convention's adoption year, the number of designated sites can change as new wetlands are added.

CMS conference at Gandhinagar

India hosted the 13th Conference of the Parties to CMS (CMS COP13) in Gandhinagar, Gujarat, from 15 to 22 February 2020, including associated meetings. The meeting addressed conservation and international cooperation for migratory species.

This was a meeting of an existing convention, not the year in which CMS was adopted. The CMS adoption year remains 1979.

Prelims focus

  • CMS or Bonn Convention: 1979; India a Party since 1983.
  • CMS Appendix I covers endangered migratory species; Appendix II concerns species requiring or benefiting from international cooperation.
  • Ramsar Convention: 1971, Ramsar in Iran; effective for India in 1982.
  • Nalsarovar became a Ramsar Site in 2012; Chhari Dhand has a designation date of 16 June 2025, with its addition announced on 30 January 2026.
  • CMS COP13 was held in Gandhinagar in 2020.
  • Trap: CMS concerns migratory species, whereas CITES concerns international trade in listed wildlife specimens.

[References: CMS Secretariat, Convention overview, Appendices I and II, India Country Profile and CMS COP13 meeting record, Gandhinagar, February 2020; Ramsar Secretariat, Convention overview and Wise Use of Wetlands; Ramsar Secretariat, India Country Profile, consulted 1 November 2026; Ramsar Secretariat, India Names an Important Bird Sanctuary in Gujarat State, Nalsarovar; Ramsar Secretariat, India Names Two More Wetlands of International Importance, 30 January 2026, Chhari Dhand; Ramsar Secretariat, India Adds Two More Wetlands of International Importance to the List, 15 October 2026; online sources consulted 1 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: Seasonal wetlands in Kachchh provide habitat for resident and migratory birds.

title: Migratory Species and Wetlands: CMS and Ramsar

body:
The Rio Earth Summit and international environmental cooperation

The United Nations Conference on Environment and Development, held in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, in 1992, is commonly called the Rio Earth Summit. It brought global attention to the need to combine environmental protection with economic and social development.

The Rio process is closely associated with 3 international conventions, often called the Rio Conventions: the Convention on Biological Diversity, the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change and the United Nations Convention to Combat Desertification.

The dates need careful distinction. CBD and UNFCCC were opened for signature at the 1992 Rio Earth Summit. UNCCD developed through the follow-up process and was adopted in 1994, not at the 1992 summit.

United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change, 1992

The United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) was adopted in 1992 and entered into force in 1994.

Its ultimate objective is to achieve stabilization of greenhouse-gas concentrations in the atmosphere at a level that would prevent dangerous human interference with the climate system. The Convention recognizes the need to achieve this objective within a time frame that allows ecosystems to adapt naturally, ensures food production is not threatened and enables sustainable economic development.

Greenhouse gases absorb and re-emit infrared radiation, influencing the Earth's energy balance. Human activities such as burning fossil fuels and deforestation can increase greenhouse-gas concentrations and contribute to climate change.

Common but differentiated responsibilities

An important principle under UNFCCC is common but differentiated responsibilities and respective capabilities, often abbreviated as CBDR-RC.

The principle recognizes that climate protection is a shared responsibility, but countries differ in their historical contributions to environmental damage and in their financial, technological and institutional capacities.

Under the Convention, developed countries are expected to take the lead in combating climate change and its adverse effects. This does not mean that developing countries have no responsibilities. Their responsibilities and the form of their commitments depend on the applicable provisions and circumstances.

India ratified UNFCCC on 1 November 1993. The Convention entered into force internationally on 21 March 1994.

UNFCCC concerns climate change. Its central environmental issue is the rise in greenhouse-gas concentrations and the resulting risks to the climate system. It is not the primary convention for controlling hazardous-waste shipments or international wildlife trade.

United Nations Convention to Combat Desertification, 1994

The United Nations Convention to Combat Desertification (UNCCD) was adopted on 17 June 1994 and entered into force on 26 December 1996.

It addresses desertification and the effects of drought through international cooperation, national action and sustainable land management, particularly in affected dryland regions.

What does desertification mean?

Under UNCCD, desertification means land degradation in arid, semi-arid and dry sub-humid areas resulting from various factors, including climatic variations and human activities.

Land degradation can include deterioration of soil, vegetation and the productive capacity of land. Relevant causes may include unsustainable cultivation, overgrazing, deforestation, erosion and other inappropriate land-management practices.

Desertification does not mean only the physical expansion of an existing sandy desert. Agricultural and grazing lands in dry regions can undergo desertification when their productive capacity deteriorates. The Convention's definition is specifically linked to arid, semi-arid and dry sub-humid areas.

UNCCD promotes measures to prevent or reduce land degradation, rehabilitate degraded land and mitigate the effects of drought. Countries develop and implement appropriate programmes and policies according to the Convention's framework.

India ratified UNCCD on 17 December 1996.

UNFCCC and UNCCD: The difference in application

FeatureUNFCCCUNCCD
Adoption year19921994
Principal concernClimate change and greenhouse gasesDesertification, dryland degradation and drought
Main approachClimate cooperation and stabilization of greenhouse-gas concentrationsSustainable land management and action against desertification
India's statusRatified in 1993Ratified in 1996

Climate change and desertification can influence each other. Higher temperatures and changing rainfall patterns may increase pressure on drylands. Degraded land may also lose vegetation and carbon-storage capacity. Nevertheless, UNFCCC is primarily a climate convention, whereas UNCCD is primarily a land-degradation and desertification convention.

Relevance to Gujarat

Parts of Kachchh and Saurashtra experience arid or semi-arid conditions and face challenges relating to water availability, soil conservation, grazing pressure and sustainable land use. Measures such as restoration of vegetation, soil and water conservation, and improved management of dryland resources illustrate the type of action relevant to UNCCD's objectives.

These are examples of the Convention's practical subject matter; they do not mean that the Convention applies only to Gujarat or that every dryland problem has the same cause.

Prelims focus

  • UNFCCC: 1992; India ratified in 1993; internationally effective in 1994.
  • UNFCCC's ultimate objective concerns stabilization of atmospheric greenhouse-gas concentrations.
  • CBDR-RC recognizes common responsibility with different responsibilities and capabilities.
  • UNCCD: 1994; India ratified in 1996.
  • Desertification concerns degradation of land in arid, semi-arid and dry sub-humid areas.
  • Trap: UNCCD is a Rio Convention, but it was adopted in 1994 rather than at the 1992 Earth Summit.

[References: NCERT, Contemporary World Politics, Class 12, Chapter 8, Environment and Natural Resources, sections on the Rio Earth Summit and Common but Differentiated Responsibility, PDF pp. 120–125 in GPSC Volume 22; NCERT, Indian Economic Development, Class 11, Chapter 9, Environment and Sustainable Development, PDF pp. 167–170 in GPSC Volume 25; UNFCCC Secretariat, United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change, Convention overview and India Ratification Status; UNCCD Secretariat, Status of Ratification, India Country Profile and Convention Article 1, Use of Terms; online sources consulted 1 November 2026.]

title: Climate Change and Desertification: UNFCCC and UNCCD

Master comparison: Convention, year, subject and India's status

The following table covers all the international environmental instruments in this lesson. The year column shows adoption, not entry into force. The membership column gives the year and form of India's participation. The status information is current to the 1 November 2026 content cutoff.

Convention or instrumentAdoptedMain subjectIndia's status
Ramsar Convention1971Conservation and wise use of wetlandsParty since 1982
CITES1973International trade in listed wild animals and plantsRatified in 1976
CMS or Bonn Convention1979Conservation of migratory wild animalsParty since 1983
Vienna Convention1985International cooperation for ozone-layer protectionAcceded in 1991
Montreal Protocol1987Phase-out of controlled ozone-depleting substancesAcceded in 1992
Basel Convention1989Transboundary movement and disposal of hazardous wastesRatified in 1992
Convention on Biological Diversity1992Biodiversity conservation, sustainable use and benefit sharingRatified in 1994
UNFCCC1992Climate change and greenhouse-gas concentrationsRatified in 1993
UNCCD1994Desertification, dryland degradation and droughtRatified in 1996
Rotterdam Convention1998PIC procedure for certain hazardous chemicals and pesticidesAcceded in 2005
Stockholm Convention2001Persistent organic pollutantsRatified in 2006
Minamata Convention2013Mercury pollutionRatified in 2018
Kigali Amendment2016Phase-down of listed HFCs under the Montreal ProtocolRatified in 2021

Distinctions that determine the correct convention

1. Ozone-depleting substances and greenhouse gases

Vienna provides the ozone-protection cooperation framework. Montreal imposes controls on ozone-depleting substances. Kigali phases down HFCs because of their climate impact. UNFCCC is the wider international framework for climate change.

2. Hazardous-waste movement and chemical trade

Basel concerns hazardous and certain other wastes moving across borders. Rotterdam concerns trade in listed hazardous chemicals and pesticides. Both may involve consent procedures, but they do not regulate the same category of material or activity.

3. Persistent pollutants and mercury

Stockholm covers listed persistent organic pollutants, with controls such as elimination, restriction and reduction of unintended releases. Minamata specifically concerns mercury and mercury compounds.

4. General biodiversity protection and international wildlife trade

CBD has broad biodiversity objectives, including sustainable use and genetic-resource benefit sharing. CITES regulates international trade in listed wildlife specimens. Neither should be confused with CMS, which promotes cooperation for migratory species.

5. Migratory animals and wetlands

CMS addresses conservation across the ranges of migratory animals. Ramsar addresses conservation and wise use of wetlands. Both may help protect migratory waterbirds, but one is species-focused and the other is habitat-focused.

6. Climate change and desertification

UNFCCC concerns greenhouse gases and the climate system. UNCCD concerns desertification and the effects of drought, especially in dryland regions. Both are linked to the Rio process but were adopted in different years.

Principal institutions and treaty mechanisms

Knowing the responsible international system helps distinguish similar abbreviations and functions.

  • Ozone Secretariat: Supports the Vienna Convention and Montreal Protocol system, including the Kigali Amendment.
  • Basel, Rotterdam and Stockholm Secretariats: Work through a coordinated secretariat arrangement for 3 related chemicals-and-waste conventions.
  • Minamata Convention Secretariat: Supports implementation of the mercury convention.
  • CBD Secretariat: Supports the Convention on Biological Diversity and its Parties.
  • CITES Secretariat: Supports international cooperation and the treaty's wildlife-trade control system.
  • CMS Secretariat: Supports cooperation for migratory wild animals.
  • Ramsar Secretariat: Supports implementation of the wetlands convention and maintenance of the international wetlands system.
  • UNFCCC and UNCCD Secretariats: Support their respective international processes on climate change and desertification.

These secretariats support treaty implementation and international coordination. They do not replace the responsibilities of national governments under the applicable conventions.

Three types of factual confusion

Adoption year versus India's joining year

Ramsar was adopted in 1971, but it became effective for India in 1982. The Kigali Amendment was adopted in 2016, while India ratified it in 2021. The same distinction must be maintained for every instrument in the table.

Framework versus specific control

Vienna establishes cooperation for ozone protection, while Montreal specifies controls on substances. CBD provides a broad biodiversity framework, while CITES specifically regulates listed-species trade. A broad environmental objective does not make all conventions legally interchangeable.

Absolute prohibition versus regulated activity

The presence of a chemical or species in an international agreement does not always mean every possible activity involving it is prohibited. CITES has different appendices, Rotterdam communicates import decisions, Stockholm permits specified exceptions, and Basel regulates transboundary waste movements under detailed conditions.

India's overall participation

As of 1 November 2026, India is a Party to the Vienna, Montreal, Stockholm, Rotterdam, Basel, Minamata, CBD, CITES, CMS, Ramsar, UNCCD and UNFCCC agreements covered here. India has also ratified the Kigali Amendment.

The distinction between a convention and an amendment remains important. The Kigali Amendment belongs to the Montreal Protocol system and should not be counted as an entirely separate convention when describing the legal relationship between the instruments.

Prelims focus

  • 1971: Ramsar; 1973: CITES; 1979: CMS.
  • 1985: Vienna; 1987: Montreal; 1989: Basel.
  • 1992: CBD and UNFCCC; 1994: UNCCD.
  • 1998: Rotterdam; 2001: Stockholm.
  • 2013: Minamata; 2016: Kigali Amendment.
  • Trap: Adoption year, international entry-into-force year and India's joining year are not the same fact.
